extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, social theory, and history of civilization; policymakers interested in social progress
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the chapter's principles explaining why some societies advance while others stagnate or decline — i.e., the claimed law(s) and conditions of human progress and retrogression. Presents social, economic, and moral conditions that promote or check civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association (integration) is the first essential of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "Association is the first essential of progress." Association (or integration) frees mental power for higher uses by permitting division of labor and economies of co-operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Association permits division of labor, storage and transmission of knowledge, specialization of occupations and functions, and the building of cumulative advantages across generations; examples include families expanding into tribes and nations, and the way association enables the accumulation of common stock of knowledge that lets a schoolboy learn more than Ptolemy knew. Anti-pattern: isolated communities lacking association cannot free mental power for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality (justice/freedom) is the second essential of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: "Equality (or justice) is the second essential of progress." Equality prevents the dissipation of mental power in conflict and in struggles for status or advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moral law and recognition of equal rights prevail, less mental power is wasted on maintenance of status or on conflict; conversely, inequality provokes aggression and wastes resources. Examples/guidance: protective tariffs, standing armies, and the difficulty of international cooperation illustrate how lack of equality dissipates collective effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental power is the motor of progress and is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental power is the instrument by which man advances; it is a fixed quantity for individuals and societies, and progress depends on the portion of mental power devoted to improvement rather than to non-progressive uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mental power is limited, social arrangements must free it (via association and equality) for scientific, technical, and moral improvement. The chapter uses metaphors such as building a pyramid on which future generations stand to show cumulative gains. Policy implication: increase the effective mental power available for improvement by reducing maintenance/conflict burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-progressive expenditures (maintenance and conflict) drain mental power
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-progressive uses of mental power are classified as maintenance (support of existence and holding advances already gained) and conflict (warfare and seeking gratification at others' expense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Societies that expend large mental resources on maintenance and conflict have less left for extending knowledge and improving methods. Practical signs: heavy militarization, legal/administrative bailing-out of dysfunction, and social arrangements that force continual attention to bare subsistence are warnings that progress will be slowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: External resistances (physical environment) constrain association and slow progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical conditions — climate, soil, geography, presence of game, deserts, mountains or arms of the sea — limit how closely men can associate and thus limit the mental power available for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilization naturally arises where nature least resists close association (e.g., rich plains and valleys). Where the environment makes subsistence costly and populations sparse, social development and specialization are constrained. Use this as an explanatory criterion for variation in rates of progress among regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warfare negates association and halts progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Warfare is the negation of association: separation into hostile tribes increases expenditure of mental power in attack and defense and checks improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronic warfare dissipates resources and undermines the social web necessary for cumulative advancement. Examples: isolated tribes in chronic hostility cannot progress; historical shifts (Roman imperial peace vs. later invasions) illustrate how loss or gain of internal peace affects progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce promotes association and therefore civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce is a form of association or co-operation that promotes civilization by building interests opposed to warfare and dispelling ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exchange creates interdependence and incentives for peaceful relations, enlarges markets for specialization, and spreads useful knowledge and techniques. Policies or conditions that foster trade and exchange will thus tend to accelerate progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion can either promote or hinder association
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion has a dual role: while religious differences have sundered men and produced warfare, common worship has at times been a basis for union and mitigated war (e.g., Greek sanctuaries, Christianity's role after Rome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the effect of religion on progress by checking whether it fosters common bonds and peaceful association or whether it erects exclusivist communities that produce separation and conflict. Example: Christianity helped maintain threads of union in Europe after Rome's fall; conversely, religion-driven animosities can perpetuate division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration and specialization tend to produce inequality unless social adjustments secure equality
rubrics_metrics.description: As societies integrate and functions specialize, there is a constant tendency toward inequality in distribution of wealth and power unless social laws and adjustments are changed to secure equality under the new conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialization creates collective powers and new values (e.g., rent) distinct from individual effort; without institutional adaptations (laws, customs, political arrangements) inequality grows and wastes mental power. Practical implication: institutional reform needed as society becomes more complex to prevent stagnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective powers arising from association can be concentrated and perpetuate injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: The collective power of society, arising with integration, is distinguishable from individual powers and tends to be lodged in the hands of a portion of the community; this unequal distribution grows by feeding on itself and blurs the idea of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for mechanisms by which patriarchal organization hardens into hereditary monarchy or oligarchy; concentration of collective power is an internal counterforce that can stop progress. Anti-patterns: institutionalized privileges, hereditary rule, and entrenched elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of habit and possibility of moral/mental deterioration impede progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Human tendencies — the power of habit to continue outdated ways and the possibility of mental and moral deterioration — enable institutions and customs to persist after they have lost usefulness and to permit growth of corrupting modes of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because habits and deterioration allow non-useful institutions to persist, societies must have mechanisms (reason, justice, reform) to correct path dependence. Signs of impending halt: rigid customs, ritualized behaviors, and institutional ossification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress is cumulative but precarious — must account for retrogression as well as advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Human progress operates by securing advances of one generation as the common property of the next, but the same processes that build civilization can create forces (internal resistances) that petrify or enervate it, causing halts or retrogressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory theory must explain both rises and falls of civilizations and why some societies assimilate new elements while others are destroyed or stagnate. Use this as a criterion when evaluating historical or policy narratives: do they explain internal and external causes of reversals as well as of growth?
